Write a vector of one type to bytes

Source: R/pack.R
bin_encode.Rd

bin_encode() writes every element of x as type, in endian order (a matrix or array in column-major order, as its elements are stored): writeBin() generalised to every width and both byte orders, rounding to f16, bf16 and f32 to nearest even, and refusing, never truncating, an integer that does not fit.

Usage

bin_encode(
  x,
  type,
  endian = c("little", "big", "native"),
  na = c("error", "allow")
)

Arguments

x

A vector: numeric, logical, integer64, complex for c64 and c128, character for s<n>, or a list of raw vectors for b<n>.

type

Any type token of bin_layout() except padding ("u8", "i128", "f16", "c64", "bool", "b16", "s8", ...), optionally with a .le or .be suffix.

endian

The byte order: "little", "big", or "native".

na

"error", or "allow" to write NA into i32 as -2^31 (and an integer64 NA into i64 as -2^63).

Value

A raw vector of length(x) times the type's width.

Details

bin_encode(bin_decode(b, t), t) is b when b is the canonical encoding of its values, which every encoding of a number is, with three exceptions. A bool byte other than 00 or 01 reads as TRUE and writes back as 01. An s<n> reads up to its first NUL, so the bytes after it write back as NULs. And an i64, u64, i128 or u128 beyond 2^53 does not decode as a double at all: ask for int64 = "integer64" (which holds 64 bits). A NaN keeps its payload through f64 and c128, but the narrower floats may not.

Examples

bin_encode(c(1, 2, 65535), "u16")
#> [1] 01 00 02 00 ff ff
bin_encode(1:3, "i32", endian = "big")
#>  [1] 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 02 00 00 00 03
bin_encode(c(0.1, 1e5), "f16")
#> [1] 66 2e 00 7c
try(bin_encode(300, "u8"))
#> Error in bin_encode() : Value 0 does not fit its type.

# bytes that are not the canonical encoding do not survive a round trip
bin_encode(bin_decode(as.raw(2), "bool"), "bool")
#> [1] 01
